title: Byte-literal comparison is normative only for project_key; agent_name/program/model/capabilities matching is undefined
claim: §2.1 states a byte-for-byte rule for `project_key` alone. The other four binding-matched fields have no comparison rule, and the §9 registry defines `request_mismatch` as a field that 'does not match' and `model_mismatch` as a model that 'does not equal' without defining match/equal. Two reasonable verifiers diverge: one compares raw bytes; another NFC-normalizes, case-folds, or trims whitespace before comparing (common defaults in Python/Go string handling). A hostile presenter exploits the lenient one by presenting `model: "Opus-4.1"` or an NFD-composed `agent_name` against a binding signed with the NFC form, passing `model_mismatch`/`request_mismatch` on the lenient verifier while the strict verifier denies. The same gap covers `capabilities`: §4.1 says they are compared 'as a set' but does not say whether element equality is byte-literal, whether duplicates in `granted_capabilities` collapse, or whether an empty-string token is a member. All 28 current vectors are host-behavior vectors, so none pins this verifier-side matching rule.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1: "`project_key` (string, **REQUIRED**) — compared **literally**, byte-for-byte, against the bundle's signed binding. The verifier **MUST NOT** apply path canonicalization"

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1: "`agent_name` (string, **REQUIRED**)" / "`program` (string, **REQUIRED**)" / "`model` (string, **REQUIRED**)" — no comparison rule attached to any of the three

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §denial-codes: "request_mismatch | a host \"request\" field does not match the signed binding, or \"granted_capabilities\" are not covered by the binding's capabilities." and "model_mismatch | the proof's committed model does not equal the requested model"
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4.1: "the verifier compares `capabilities` as a set for authorization, but the *signed bytes* are order-sensitive."

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §request: "This byte-literal rule is a subtle interoperability hazard and is stated explicitly to prevent a verifier from silently normalizing a project key." — the stated rationale applies equally to the four fields the rule does not cover
Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): 28 vectors, all kind host_behavior; no verifier-side matching vector exists
proposed_artifact: A spec-hardening diff pinned to a4f546f that generalizes the byte-literal, no-normalization rule to all five binding-matched request fields, defines capability set membership as byte-literal element equality with duplicate tokens in `granted_capabilities` collapsed and the empty string treated as an ordinary token, and adds matching text to draft-kondoju-evc-01 §request and the §denial-codes rows for request_mismatch/model_mismatch.

title: retain_until has no lower bound; a past-dated or zero retain_until lets a TTL-store host satisfy 'retain until' by never reserving
claim: The closed verdict schema types `retain_until` as a bare integer with no `minimum`, so `0`, a negative value, or a timestamp already in the past passes schema validation and reaches the reserve-before-act path. The normative host obligation is phrased as retention 'until' `retain_until`. A lazy host backed by a TTL store (Redis SET NX EX, DynamoDB TTL, in-memory expiry map) computes ttl = retain_until - now, gets a value ≤ 0, and either skips the insert or inserts an entry the store evicts immediately; on a literal reading the 'retain until' obligation is already satisfied. The same `allow` + `consume_nonces` verdict presented twice in the same second is then allowed twice. A host that inserts unconditionally and only garbage-collects later denies the second run. This is distinct from the previously rejected unbounded-window finding (upper bound / storage growth): the divergence here is at the lower bound and produces an actual replay, not a retention cost. The current vectors (`host-nonce-reserve-novel-allow`, `host-nonce-reserve-replay-deny`, `host-nonce-reserve-all-any-conflict-deny`) all use a far-future `retain_until` (4102444800 in the §3.2 example), so a TTL-skipping host passes the suite.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 verdict schema: "\"retain_until\": { \"type\": \"integer\" }" — no minimum, exclusiveMinimum, or relation to now_unix
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: "`retain_until` (integer, **REQUIRED**) — Unix seconds until which the host **MUST** retain the consumed nonce."

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §terminology: "reserve-before-act: The host obligation, in host nonce mode, to durably reserve every returned nonce with unique-insert semantics before performing the privileged action (Section 7)." — reservation and retention are stated as one obligation, so a zero-length retention reads as a zero-length reservation

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2 example uses "retain_until": 4102444800 (year 2100); vector index 0.6.0 lists only novel / replay / all-any-conflict reserve cases, none with retain_until ≤ now
Runnable: `npx @bolyra/evc-conformance --host "<cmd>"` against a host whose nonce store is a TTL map; expected to pass 28/28 today while replaying a retain_until=0 nonce
proposed_artifact: Two new host_behavior conformance vectors for `spec/fixtures/host-conformance/` — `host-nonce-reserve-retain-until-zero-replay-deny` (retain_until: 0) and `host-nonce-reserve-retain-until-past-replay-deny` (retain_until: now_unix - 1), each running the identical allow twice and requiring the second run to fail closed as a replay — plus a one-sentence spec hardening pinned to a4f546f that a host MUST perform the unique-insert reservation regardless of the `retain_until` value and MUST retain at least until the end of its own action, with a bump of the vector-set version.

title: Spec does not state whether the unique-insert key is `nonce` alone or (issuer_key, nonce); a composite-keyed host replays under a changed issuer_key
claim: §3.2 says `issuer_key` 'scopes the nonce namespace' and in the same breath that it is 'for host bookkeeping only' because the nonce is 'already globally unique'. A hostile or merely conventional implementer reads 'scopes the namespace' and builds the nonce table with a composite primary key (issuer_key, nonce) — the natural schema for a scoped namespace. The reference-style reading keys on `nonce` alone. The two diverge on the run where the same `nonce` string arrives with a different `issuer_key` (a second verifier binary that formats the key differently, a decimal-vs-hex rendering change between verifier versions, or a presenter-influenced value if a verifier echoes anything from the bundle): the composite-keyed host inserts a fresh row and allows; the nonce-keyed host denies as a replay. A related unstated case is two entries in ONE `consume_nonces` list carrying the same `nonce`: a host that dedups before inserting allows, a host that inserts sequentially with unique-insert semantics conflicts with itself and denies. No current vector varies `issuer_key` across runs or repeats a nonce within a list; `host-nonce-reserve-replay-deny` replays the byte-identical verdict.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: "`issuer_key` (string, **REQUIRED**) — the issuer/operator key that scopes the nonce namespace. For host bookkeeping only; the `nonce` is already globally unique (§8)." — 'scopes the namespace' and 'bookkeeping only' pull an implementer in opposite directions

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.3: "the host **MUST** reserve **every** entry in the list **before** performing the privileged a…" (reserve-each is stated; the identity of the uniqueness key is not)

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §architecture pseudocode: "if not reserve_nonce_atomically(entry): reject(\"replay\")" — `entry` (the whole object) is passed, which a literal implementer reads as the tuple being the key

Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): `host-nonce-reserve-replay-deny` — "the same allow+consume_nonces verdict, but the nonce…" (byte-identical replay only); no vector varies issuer_key or repeats a nonce within one list
Runnable: `npx @bolyra/evc-conformance --host "<cmd>"` against a host using a composite (issuer_key, nonce) unique index; passes today
proposed_artifact: Two new host_behavior conformance vectors — `host-nonce-reserve-replay-different-issuer-key-deny` (run 1: issuer_key K1 / nonce N allowed; run 2: issuer_key K2 / same nonce N MUST fail closed) and `host-nonce-reserve-duplicate-nonce-in-list` (one allow whose two entries share a nonce, pinning the expected outcome) — plus a spec-hardening diff pinned to a4f546f stating that the unique-insert key is the `nonce` string alone and that `issuer_key` MUST NOT participate in uniqueness, with the same sentence added to draft-kondoju-evc-01 Section 7.

title: Request-write failure (EPIPE) when the verifier exits before consuming stdin is not a listed §7.2 condition; hosts crash, deny, or relay
claim: §2 obligates the host to write the whole request then close stdin, and §6 obligates the verifier to stop reading at its bound and emit `malformed_input` — which means a conforming verifier will routinely exit while the host is still writing a large request, closing the pipe under the host's write. §7.2's enumerated fail-closed conditions cover exit status, timeout, signal death, and stdout shape, but not failure of the host's own request delivery. Three reasonable hosts diverge: (1) a Node host with no `error` listener on `child.stdin` gets an unhandled EPIPE and crashes the host process — no decision at all, a trivial denial-of-service against the host by any verifier that exits early; (2) a host that aborts on the write error denies before ever reading a schema-valid verdict; (3) a host that swallows the error reads stdout and relays whatever is there, including an `allow` from a verifier that demonstrably never read the request. The spec's own bound guarantees case (1)/(2)/(3) is reachable with a legitimate oversize request, and the lazy-verifier variant (emit allow, never read stdin) is the interesting hostile case: EPIPE is the one signal the host has that the request was not consumed, and the spec neither requires nor forbids acting on it. No vector exercises a verifier that exits before draining stdin; every current fixture has the verifier read stdin first.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2: "The host **MUST** write exactly one JSON object, UTF-8 encoded, to the verifier's stdin and then **MUST** close (EOF) stdin."

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §6: "A request over the bound **MUST** yield `deny code=malformed_input`; the verifier **MUST NOT** buffer an unbounded request." — a conforming verifier therefore stops reading and exits mid-write

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2 enumerates: non-zero exit; timeout; death by signal / crash; unparseable, empty, oversized, or multi-object stdout; unknown verdict / missing deny fields; schema failure — a failed request write is absent
spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §architecture pseudocode: "write(child.stdin, json(request)); close(child.stdin)" with no failure branch, unlike every downstream step which has an explicit reject()

Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): `host-deny-no-output-timeout` — "the verifier reads stdin, writes nothing…"; `host-deny-partial-json-timeout`, `host-deny-oversize-stdout` — all fixtures consume stdin before misbehaving; none exits before stdin is drained

Runnable: `npx @bolyra/evc-conformance --host "<cmd>"` with a proposed fixture verifier `exec 0<&-; printf '{"verdict":"deny","code":"malformed_input","message":"unread"}'; exit 0` driven with a request whose bundle exceeds the OS pipe buffer (≥ 256 KiB) so the host's write cannot complete before the close
proposed_artifact: Two new host_behavior conformance vectors — `host-relay-deny-verifier-exits-before-stdin-drained` (oversize request, verifier closes stdin unread and emits a schema-valid `malformed_input` deny at exit 0; the host MUST reach a deny and MUST NOT crash or hang) and `host-deny-allow-with-stdin-unread` (same early close but the verifier emits `allow`; pins the expected outcome) — plus a spec-hardening diff pinned to a4f546f adding request-write failure to the §7.2 list and the draft pseudocode, and stating that a host MUST survive EPIPE on stdin and treat a write failure as fail-closed under its own classification.

title: No vector for a verifier that writes a complete, schema-valid `allow` and is then killed by an unsolicited signal
claim: §7.2 lists 'death by signal / crash' as an unconditional deny and §7.2 precedence text requires `signal_death` to be classified distinctly from `nonzero_exit`, but the only signal vector in set 0.6.0 (`host-deny-killed-by-signal`) kills the verifier BEFORE any output. The exit-code sibling (`host-deny-nonzero-exit-after-allow`) exists, the signal sibling does not. That is exactly the ordering a lazy host gets wrong: it parses stdout first, sees a perfect `{"verdict":"allow"}\n`, then checks the exit status with a comparison that treats a signal death as success. In Node the `close` event delivers `code === null` when the child died by signal, so `if (code > 0) deny()` is skipped; in Python `returncode` is negative (`-11` for SIGSEGV), so the same `> 0` guard also passes. Both are fail-open on a verdict the spec says MUST be denied. The attack is a verifier whose native proof library segfaults or is OOM-killed in teardown after the verdict flush (§5.1 explicitly anticipates native libraries misbehaving on fd 1; nothing says they finish exiting cleanly), or a presenter who can influence verifier teardown timing. Observable a vector can assert: verifier writes `{"verdict":"allow"}\n`, flushes, then raises SIGSEGV on itself; host MUST deny and, if it reports a class, MUST report `signal_death`, not `allow` and not `nonzero_exit`.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2: 'The host MUST treat all of the following as deny, regardless of what (if anything) reached stdout: ... death by signal / crash;'

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2: 'death by an unsolicited signal and a non-zero exit are distinct conditions (`signal_death` vs `nonzero_exit`, §16.3) — a host MUST NOT collapse them into one classification.'

Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): 'host-deny-killed-by-signal: ... the verifier terminates via an unsolicited fatal signal before produ[cing output]' and 'host-deny-nonzero-exit-after-allow: the verifier prints a syntactically valid `allow` and then ex[its non-zero]' — no vector combines a complete allow with a subsequent signal death.

Node.js child_process docs, 'close' event: 'code <number> The exit code if the child exited on its own... null if the process was killed by a signal' — https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html#event-close
Python subprocess docs: 'A negative value -N indicates that the child was terminated by signal N (POSIX only)' — https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen.returncode

Reproduce the fail-open host pattern in an isolated scratch dir: `node -e "const {spawn}=require('child_process');const c=spawn('sh',['-c','printf \\'{\"verdict\":\"allow\"}\\n\\'; kill -SEGV $$']);let o='';c.stdout.on('data',d=>o+=d);c.on('close',(code,sig)=>{console.log('code',code,'signal',sig,'naive-verdict',(code>0)?'deny':JSON.parse(o).verdict)})"` — prints `code null signal SIGSEGV naive-verdict allow`.
proposed_artifact: A new host_behavior conformance vector `host-deny-signal-death-after-allow` (verifier stub emits a complete newline-terminated `allow`, flushes, then self-delivers SIGSEGV; expected decision deny, expected failure class `signal_death`) staged as a fixture diff pinned to a4f546f, plus the matching one-line addition to the §16.3 offered-case list.

title: Mode confusion: a host running in local nonce mode has no normative obligation when a verdict carries `consume_nonces`
claim: §3.2 says `consume_nonces` is 'Emitted only in host nonce mode', and §7.3 scopes reserve-before-act to 'When the host runs the verifier in host nonce mode'. Neither the contract nor the draft says what a host that believes it is in LOCAL nonce mode must do when an `allow` arrives carrying `consume_nonces`. The draft's pseudocode reserves unconditionally (`for entry in (verdict.consume_nonces or [])`), but pseudocode is non-normative and the prose lets a host that 'is not in host nonce mode' treat the field as inert metadata on a schema-valid allow and proceed. That is a fail-open replay window: the verifier believed the host would burn the nullifier, the host believed the verifier had burned it, and nobody did. It is reachable by ordinary misconfiguration (verifier launched with the host-mode flag, host config left in local mode), by a verifier that is host-mode-only by design (the classical hosted-verify class returns nonces it cannot store locally), or by a mixed fan-out where one of several verifiers is host-mode. The fix is a single MUST: a host MUST apply §7.3 to every `consume_nonces` list it receives regardless of the mode it believes it configured, and a host unable to reserve (no durable store) MUST treat the verdict as deny (`schema_invalid`/`replay` class), never as a bare allow. Observable: with the HUT started with the nonce store disabled/absent (the local-mode configuration the runner already distinguishes for the existing reserve vectors), the verifier stub returns the fixed allow+consume_nonces twice; the host MUST NOT emit two allows.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: 'Emitted only in host nonce mode (§8). Instructs the host to durably record each one-time nonce so the same proof cannot be replayed.'

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.3: 'When the host runs the verifier in host nonce mode (§8) and receives `allow` with `consume_nonces`, the host MUST reserve every entry in the list before performing the privileged a[ction]' — the obligation is conditioned on the host's own belief about its mode, not on the presence of the field.

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §3 pseudocode: 'for entry in (verdict.consume_nonces or []):        // Sec 7 host mode / if not reserve_nonce_atomically(entry): reject("replay")   // reserve ALL' — unconditional in code, conditional in prose; the draft labels the pseudocode 'Language-neutral pseudocode', not normative.

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md Terminology: 'host nonce mode / local nonce mode: The two replay-protection modes (Section 7). In local mode the verifier owns the durable nonce store; in host mode the verifier returns nonces for the host to reserve.' — no rule for the cross case.
Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): the three `host-nonce-reserve-*` vectors all presuppose the HUT is in host nonce mode; no vector drives a local-mode HUT with a nonce-bearing allow.
proposed_artifact: A spec-hardening diff pinned to a4f546f adding one normative paragraph to §7.3 (and the mirrored sentence in draft-kondoju-evc-01 §7) making reserve-before-act unconditional on field presence, with a companion vector `host-deny-consume-nonces-in-local-mode-replay` asserting a local-mode HUT never allows the same consume_nonces verdict twice.

title: `retain_until` has no lower bound: a value at or before `now_unix` makes the retention MUST vacuous and licenses immediate eviction
claim: Refinement of the iteration-1 retain_until finding (that one was dropped for staging language, not on merit; this narrows it to the exploitable lower boundary and stays in staging language). The verdict schema types `retain_until` as a bare `integer` with no minimum, and §3.2's only obligation is 'Unix seconds until which the host MUST retain the consumed nonce'. If `retain_until <= now_unix` (or 0, or negative) that obligation is satisfied at the instant of reservation, so a host with an ordinary TTL-based store (Redis `EXPIREAT`, a DynamoDB TTL attribute, a periodic sweeper) legitimately evicts the nonce before the privileged action even completes, and a second presentation of the same bundle within the same second is a novel insert: fail-open replay. `now_unix` is host-supplied (§2.1), so the host can detect the condition locally without trusting the verifier's clock. A verifier that emits `retain_until <= now_unix` is internally inconsistent (its own retention horizon has already passed), which is the §7.2 'fails the verdict schema' class, not a policy decision. Proposed rule: `retain_until` MUST be strictly greater than the request's `now_unix`; a host MUST treat an entry violating this as a schema-invalid verdict and fail closed. Observables for vectors: (a) allow with `retain_until: 0` → deny/schema_invalid; (b) allow with `retain_until: now_unix - 1` → deny/schema_invalid; (c) allow with `retain_until: now_unix + 1`, then the identical verdict re-presented → second MUST deny (guards against a host that reserves but evicts on the same tick).
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: '`retain_until` (integer, REQUIRED) — Unix seconds until which the host MUST retain the consumed nonce.'
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 verdict schema: '"retain_until": { "type": "integer" }' — contrast with the request schema, which bounds `now_unix` with '"exclusiveMinimum": 0'.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1: '`now_unix` ... The verifier MUST evaluate credential expiry against this value, not against its own clock, so the host owns the time source.' — the host therefore has the reference value needed to check `retain_until > now_unix` locally.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2: the host MUST deny 'a verdict that otherwise fails the §3.4 verdict schema ... or any disallowed additional property' — value-range violations on `retain_until` are not currently a schema failure because the schema has no range.
Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): `host-deny-nonce-entry-wrong-type` covers a string in an integer slot; no vector exercises an in-range-typed but past/zero/negative `retain_until`.
Redis EXPIREAT semantics: 'A timestamp in the past will delete the key immediately' — https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/expireat/
proposed_artifact: A spec-hardening diff pinned to a4f546f adding `retain_until MUST be > now_unix` to §3.2 and `"exclusiveMinimum": 0` to the §3.4 schema, plus three host_behavior vectors (`host-deny-retain-until-zero`, `host-deny-retain-until-past`, `host-nonce-reserve-retain-until-min-replay-deny`) staged as fixture diffs with the sync.js note.

title: Empty-string `nonce` / `issuer_key` are schema-valid, and the most common host idioms silently skip or fail to unique-insert them
claim: The consume_nonces entry schema types `nonce` and `issuer_key` as `string` with no `minLength`, unlike the request's `bundle` which carries `minLength: 1`. An `allow` with `"nonce": ""` is therefore a schema-valid verdict the host MUST honor by reserving it. Two ubiquitous host idioms turn that into fail-open: (1) a guard like `if (!entry.nonce) continue;` in JavaScript, or `if not entry["nonce"]: continue` in Python, treats the empty string as absent and skips reservation entirely, then proceeds on the allow; (2) a SQL unique-insert store on Oracle treats `''` as NULL, and a single-column UNIQUE index admits unlimited NULL rows, so every presentation inserts successfully and no replay is ever detected. Neither host violates a stated MUST today. The gap is doubly exploitable because the agent nullifier is verifier-derived: a verifier bug that renders a nullifier as `""` for one credential class (for example an unset optional human nullifier serialized as `human:` with an empty hash) produces a permanently replayable bundle under hosts that pass all 28 current vectors. Observable a vector can assert: verifier stub returns `{"verdict":"allow","consume_nonces":[{"issuer_key":"k","nonce":"","retain_until":4102444800}]}`; under the proposed `minLength: 1` the host MUST deny `schema_invalid`; under the current schema the runner can at minimum assert that presenting the identical verdict twice yields deny on the second run.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 verdict schema, consume_nonces item: '"properties": { "issuer_key": { "type": "string" }, "nonce": { "type": "string" }, "retain_until": { "type": "integer" } }' — no `minLength`.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.2 request schema, for contrast: '"bundle": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 }' — the spec already knows to forbid empty strings where emptiness is meaningless, but only on the request side.
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: '`nonce` (string, REQUIRED) — the one-time value the host MUST record.' and §7.3 'reserve ... EACH entry' — an empty string is an entry.

Conformance vector index (set 0.6.0): `host-deny-malformed-consume-nonce` covers an OMITTED required field and `host-deny-nonce-entry-wrong-type` covers a wrong JSON type; neither covers a present, correctly-typed, empty string.

Oracle Database SQL Language Reference, 'Nulls': 'Oracle Database currently treats a character value with a length of zero as null' — https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/sqlrf/Nulls.html ; combined with unique-constraint semantics that permit multiple all-NULL rows, `''` never conflicts.

Reproduce the falsy-skip idiom in an isolated scratch dir: `node -e "const v={verdict:'allow',consume_nonces:[{issuer_key:'k',nonce:'',retain_until:4102444800}]};const seen=new Set();let ok=true;for(const e of v.consume_nonces){if(!e.nonce)continue;if(seen.has(e.nonce)){ok=false;break}seen.add(e.nonce)}console.log('reserved',seen.size,'decision',ok?'proceed':'deny')"` — prints `reserved 0 decision proceed` for a verdict the spec says required a reservation.
proposed_artifact: A staged diff pinned to a4f546f adding `"minLength": 1` to `nonce` and `issuer_key` in the §3.4 schema (mirrored in draft-kondoju-evc-01 Appendix schemas), plus two host_behavior vectors `host-deny-empty-nonce-string` and `host-deny-empty-issuer-key` with the sync.js regeneration note.

title: The allow branch of the closed verdict schema forbids `detail`, so a conforming verifier cannot return non-secret provenance (effective scope, expiry, delegation depth) that OAuth-style `act` chains and APS passports expose to the enforcement point
claim: draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-03 builds delegation on RFC 8693 token exchange, where the `act` claim (RFC 8693 §4.1) gives the enforcing party an auditable actor chain on a successful authorization, and an APS passport is itself the disclosed record of who is acting under which scope. EVC v1's `allow` is information-free by construction: §3.4's allow branch enumerates only `verdict`, `kind`, `consume_nonces` with `additionalProperties: false`, while the deny branch gets an OPTIONAL `detail` object. A host therefore cannot log which credential expiry, effective scope, or delegation depth produced the allow, even though the product surface is 'proving who authorized an action, at what limit, for which payee'. The asymmetry is not a security necessity: `detail` on deny is already specified as logging-only and non-secret, and the `kind` field was added to the closed schema in the 2026-07-10 revision without a wire-major bump, with the stated caveat that pre-revision hosts fail closed on it. The same precedent covers an OPTIONAL, explicitly non-authorizing `detail` on allow.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4, allow branch: `"required": ["verdict"], "additionalProperties": false, "properties": { "verdict": { "const": "allow" }, "kind": ..., "consume_nonces": ... }` — no `detail` property; deny branch: `"detail": { "type": "object" }`.
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.3: '`detail` (object, OPTIONAL) — structured context for logs/debugging. A verifier SHOULD echo the originating internal error code here'.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.5: 'such verifiers are introduced by the 2026-07-10 revision, §15; no non-`zk` verifier existed under the original v1' and 'a host validating against the original (pre-revision) closed v1 schema rejects any `kind`-bearing verdict (§11)' — precedent for an additive OPTIONAL field inside wire major 1.

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md informative reference I-D.klrc-aiagent-auth (draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-03, 2026-07-06), https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-klrc-aiagent-auth/ ; RFC 8693 §4.1 defines the `act` (actor) claim chain that survives to the resource server on success.

Conformance vector host-deny-allow-extra-property (set 0.6.0) pins the current behavior: an allow with any additional property is a host fail-closed condition, so any -02 change must ship with a vector update.

title: All 28 conformance vectors test the host's handling of verifier stdout; none tests the host's own §2 request obligations (single object, stdin EOF, required fields, positive integer now_unix), which AuthZEN-style PEP/PDP interop tests on both sides
claim: The AuthZEN family (COAZ/AARP, already a threat card) publishes interop testing where the PEP's request is validated against the request schema, not just the PDP's response. EVC's host-conformance suite is asymmetric: every vector in set 0.6.0 is a verdict-side stimulus (malformed stdout, timeout, signal, nonce reserve). A host that never closes stdin, writes two request objects, omits `granted_capabilities`, or sends `now_unix` as a float or string can still pass 28/28, because the fixture verifiers never assert anything about the bytes they received. Since SPEC HARDNESS is scored on the fraction of normative MUSTs covered by a vector, the §2 host MUSTs are an uncovered block. The gap is closable without a wire change: a request-validating fixture verifier reads stdin to EOF, parses exactly one object, checks the §2.2 schema, and returns `allow` only if the host's request was conformant, otherwise `deny code=malformed_input`. The expected host outcome flips: a non-conforming host observes a deny and the runner records a FAIL on a vector whose expected decision is allow.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2: 'The host MUST write exactly one JSON object, UTF-8 encoded, to the verifier's stdin and then MUST close (EOF) stdin. The host MUST NOT write more than one object, trailing bytes, or a stream of objects.'
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1: '`now_unix` (integer, REQUIRED, positive)' and '`granted_capabilities` (array of strings, REQUIRED) ... An empty array is permitted.'

Conformance vector index, set 0.6.0: 28 vectors, all named host-allow-* / host-deny-* / host-nonce-*, each described as a verifier stdout/exit/nonce stimulus; no vector description mentions the request the host wrote.

title: AERF v0.1 (Agent Evidence Receipt Format, aerf-spec/agentmint-python) declares a stable tamper-evident record format for agent actions; EVC specifies no durable decision record at the enforcement point, leaving the receipt layer to a separate package
claim: As an AERF author I would argue the enforcement boundary is only half the story: a verdict that is not bound into an independently verifiable record cannot be audited after the fact, and AERF's notarize/verify/export CLI ships that record as the primary artifact with the format declared stable. EVC v1 explicitly excludes durable records ('EVC is deliberately not a governance framework'), and the wire verdict carries no decision identifier or request digest, so the host↔verifier exchange leaves no first-class evidence. The overlap is with @bolyra/receipts (ES256K, hash-chained, instance-bound, v0.11.0), not with EVC itself, which makes this a positioning threat rather than a spec break: if AERF becomes the receipt vocabulary hosts adopt, EVC hosts will emit AERF records around Bolyra verdicts and the receipts package loses the slot. Counter available: a public field-by-field comparison showing @bolyra/receipts already covers hash-chaining, signer binding, and `commerce.intentHash`, and a documented mapping from an EVC verdict plus request to a receipt, published as spec-level guidance rather than a build plan.

title: IANA Considerations: a registry closed by wire-major bump is not an IANA registry (RFC 8126 policy missing) — -02 blocker
claim: The draft simultaneously declares the 15-code deny table 'the candidate IANA registry' and forbids any addition/removal/rename without a wire-major version bump. Under RFC 8126 an IANA registry exists precisely so values can be added under a stated registration policy without republishing the document; a table whose only change mechanism is a new major of this document is a normative in-document enumeration, not a registry. The same closure applies to the three-member `kind` enum and the integer `version`. As written, an IANA reviewer or IESG last-call review will return the section: either (a) state 'This document has no IANA actions' and keep §denial-codes as the sole normative closed enumeration (consistent with the closed JSON Schema `enum`), or (b) create 'EVC Denial Codes' and 'EVC Verifier Kinds' registries with RFC 8126 policy **Standards Action** (or Specification Required + Designated Expert) and a 'Change Controller: IETF' field, and explicitly reconcile that with the closed-schema rule by saying new registrations take effect only in a new wire major. The `$id` URLs in the schemas (https://bolyra.ai/spec/...) also need a note that they are identifiers, not dereferenced, or migration to a stable URN.

draft-kondoju-evc-01 §denial-codes: "Within a wire major, this registry is closed: the deny schema ({{schemas}}) enumerates exactly these codes, so a verdict carrying any other \"code\" fails the verdict schema and the host MUST fail closed"

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 verdict schema pins `"code": {"type":"string","enum":[...15 values...]}` and `"kind": {"type":"string","enum":["classical","zk","external"]}` with `additionalProperties: false`

RFC 8126 §4 (registration policies) and §2.2 (registry change-control fields): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8126#section-4
proposed_artifact: A staged diff to draft-kondoju-evc-01's IANA Considerations replacing the 'candidate registry' language with a concrete RFC 8126 registry definition (name, fields, Standards Action policy, initial contents = the 15 codes and 3 kinds, change controller) and a one-sentence reconciliation with the closed-schema/wire-major rule, plus a non-dereferencing note on the schema `$id` URIs.

title: Binding canonicalization is defined by normative reference to an npm package instead of RFC 8785 (JCS) — reference hygiene / -02 blocker
claim: §4.1 of the contract (transcribed as Appendix B of the draft, and load-bearing for the `invalid_signature` code) states that any implementer MUST reproduce exact bytes, then defines the canonical form as 'the sorted-key, compact JSON serialization defined by `@bolyra/receipts` (`canonicalize`)'. That is a downward normative reference to a vendor implementation, not to a stable specification. Sorted-key compact JSON is underspecified without a spec: key sort order (UTF-16 code units per RFC 8785 vs. code points vs. bytes), string escaping (`\u` forms, non-ASCII, `/`), number serialization (RFC 8785 uses ECMAScript Number::toString; `expiry` and `retain_until` as integers are fine but large or float-typed inputs are not), and treatment of duplicate members. A Rust or Go implementer reading the draft alone cannot guarantee byte identity and will fail with `invalid_signature` on strings containing non-ASCII in `project_key` or `agent_name`. Resolution: cite RFC 8785 JCS as the normative canonicalization (moving it to the normative reference list), state any deliberate divergence, and add a conformance vector whose binding contains a non-ASCII `project_key` and a key whose sort order differs between code-unit and code-point ordering.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4: "Any implementer that produces or verifies a bundle **MUST** reproduce these exact bytes."

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4.1: "where `canonicalize` is the sorted-key, compact (no insignificant whitespace) JSON serialization defined by `@bolyra/receipts` (`canonicalize`). Object keys **MUST** be sorted; array elements (including `capabilities`) **MUST NOT** be reordered."
draft-kondoju-evc-01 §denial-codes row: "invalid_signature | the request-binding signature (Appendix B) did not verify against the proven operator key."
draft-kondoju-evc-01 references block lists only RFC2119, RFC8174, RFC8259 as normative; RFC 8785 is absent from both normative and informative lists.
RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme §3.2.3 (property sorting by UTF-16 code units) and §3.2.2.3 (number serialization): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785
proposed_artifact: A staged diff to the contract §4.1 and the draft's Appendix B + references that defines canonicalization by normative reference to RFC 8785 (with explicit divergence statements, if any, checked against the pinned `@bolyra/receipts` canonicalize source), plus one new conformance-vector proposal exercising non-ASCII and code-unit-vs-code-point key ordering in the signed binding.

title: Architecture pseudocode is not marked informative and contradicts the §7.2 failure-classification precedence and the closed verdict schema
claim: Refinement of the iteration-1 candidate that was dropped on artifact shape, not merit. The draft's Section 3 pseudocode is introduced only as 'Language-neutral pseudocode for the host side' with no RFC-style '(non-normative)' marker, so a reader may treat it as the implementation of the MUSTs. It diverges from the normative text in three checkable ways: (1) it tests `status != 0` before `timed_out(child)`, whereas the contract's §7.2 precedence for reported classification is output-bound kill, then timeout, then signal death, then non-zero exit, then parse/schema — and §7.2 says a host MUST NOT collapse signal death and non-zero exit, yet the pseudocode has no signal-death branch at all; (2) `for entry in (verdict.consume_nonces or [])` silently accepts an empty `consume_nonces` array that the closed §3.4 schema (`minItems: 1`) requires the host to reject (vector host-deny-empty-consume-nonces); (3) no schema-validation step appears between parse and the switch, so an unrecognized `kind`, an extra property, or an out-of-registry `code` would be relayed — the exact relay behavior §denial-codes now forbids. The fix is textual: label the block '(informative)', add a `validate_schema(verdict) or reject("schema_invalid")` step, add a `signaled(child)` branch, and reorder branches to match §7.2 or add a sentence that ordering in the sketch is illustrative and §7.2 governs.
evidence: draft-kondoju-evc-01 §Architecture: "Language-neutral pseudocode for the host side:" followed by `if status != 0: reject("non-zero exit")` then `if timed_out(child): reject("timeout")` then `verdict = parse_single_json_object(out)` then `for entry in (verdict.consume_nonces or []):` — no signal-death branch, no schema check.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2: "classify the cause it acted on in this precedence: its own kills first (output bound, then timeout), then an unsolicited signal death, then a non-zero exit, and only then the stdout parse and schema checks ... a host **MUST NOT** collapse them into one classification."
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 allow schema: `"consume_nonces": {"type":"array","minItems":1, ...}` with `"additionalProperties": false`

title: Mechanical host-side MUST → conformance-vector coverage map at the pinned commit, exposing which normative host obligations have no vector
claim: SPEC HARDNESS is scored partly on '% of normative MUSTs covered by a conformance vector', but no reproducible artifact enumerates the host-side MUSTs and maps each to a vector id. Reading §2, §5.2, §7.2 and §7.3 against the 28-vector index, at least four host obligations have no vector: (1) §2 'MUST close (EOF) stdin' after exactly one object; (2) §7.2 'MUST NOT collapse [signal_death and nonzero_exit] into one classification' — the two vectors exist but the index does not show that the CLASS STRING is asserted; (3) §7.3 reserve 'before performing the privileged action' — the nonce vectors assert reservation but not ordering relative to the action; (4) §5.2 'stdout that is empty' — the index has non-JSON, binary, leading/trailing garbage and multi-object cases but no empty-stdout-at-exit-0 vector. A skeptical reviewer will ask for the map, not the percentage.
